question: Look at the compare-contrast essay given below and pay attention to its elements.
answer:
THE ELEMENTS OF THE MODEL COMPARE-CONTRAST ESSAY

1. Topic — “Basketball and Football”. The essay compares two items of the same class (team games played with a ball), which is the first requirement of a fair comparison.

2. Introduction (developing a ground) — “Basketball and football are sports with many similarities and differences. Both sports are fun and each has many beneficial properties. Here are some of the similarities and differences between basketball and football.” Developing a ground means opening with what the two subjects share (both are fun, both are beneficial) before the essay separates them; the last sentence announces the plan.

3. Body — similarities. “Basketball and football are played with a round ball. Both offer many cardiovascular activities like running. So, if anyone wants to get in shape, these are the sports she/he needs to play. A referee judges each match. If a player breaks the rules, he will be called upon to commit a fault… After all, a score is kept in every game.”

4. Body — differences. “An athlete dribbles the ball in both sports, a basketball player uses his hands and a footballer uses his feet. Usually, football is played outdoors on a large field and indoor but basketball on a wooden field. Basketball is played with 5 players and football has 11. After all, basketball has four quarters and football has two halves.”

5. Connectors. Within the body: “Both”, “So”, “After all”, “Similarly”, “Although … yet”, “Usually”, “but”, “and”. In the conclusion: “To sum up”, “also”. These are the words that signal a similarity (both, similarly, like) or a difference (although, however, but, whereas).

6. Conclusion — “To sum up, both sports are fun and exciting to play. Each sports offers activity and competitiveness. They are also one of a kind. Both games are like heart of outdoor games.” It returns to the opening idea, sums up the comparison in one sentence and closes with a figure of speech.

7. Metaphor — the book labels “Both games are like heart of outdoor games” as a metaphor. Strictly it is a simile, because it uses “like”; a metaphor would say “Both games are the heart of outdoor games”. The phrase also needs the article: “the heart of outdoor games”.
explanation: This is an analysis task, not a writing task: the answer names each labelled element of the sample (topic, introduction that develops a ground, body of similarities and differences, connectors, conclusion, metaphor) and quotes the words that carry it. The bold phrases in the table are the connectors and the metaphor, which is why the teacher’s note asks the class to collect them.

question: Work individually, and identify some elements of comparison and contrast in the given essay below.
answer:
ELEMENTS OF COMPARISON AND CONTRAST IN THE ESSAY ON METHODS OF COMMUNICATION

1. Subject of comparison — current versus previous methods of communication: two items of one class, one in the past and one in the present.

2. Point of similarity (paragraph 1). Topic sentence: “One similarity between current and previous methods of communication relates to the form of communication.” Details: in the past, written forms (letters) were used beside oral forms (telephone calls); today “people now-a-days use both of these forms”. Connector: “Similarly”.

3. First difference — speed (paragraph 2). Signal: “However, there are clearly many differences … the most notable of which is speed.” Detail: “In the past, letters would take days to arrive at their destination”, whereas today a message arrives at once. Connector of contrast: “However”.

4. Second difference — range of methods (paragraph 3). Signal: “Another significant difference is the range of communication methods.” Details: the past had “primarily the telephone and the letter”; today there is “a vast array of communication methods”. Connectors: “By comparison”, “not only … but also”, “such as”.

5. Conclusion (paragraph 4). Signal: “In conclusion”. It restates the one similarity (“the forms of communication”) and the two differences (“the speed of communication and the range of communication tools available”), then adds a comment and a prediction: technology “will surely continue progressing in future; besides, the advanced tools which we use today may one day also become outdated.”

6. Language of comparison and contrast used in the essay — “One similarity”, “Similarly”, “both of these forms”, “However”, “differences”, “the most notable of which”, “Another significant difference”, “By comparison”, “not only … but also”, “While there are some similarities …, there are significant differences”, “In conclusion”.

7. Organisation — point by point: one similarity is given first, then difference 1 (speed), then difference 2 (range of tools), and finally a conclusion. Each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence, supports it with examples and links to the next with a connector.
explanation: Open-ended identification task. A complete answer names the subject, the single similarity, the two differences (speed and range of tools), the conclusion that restates them, and the connectors that signal each move. Wording may vary; the elements and quotations should not.

question: Work with a partner and write compare-contrast essay on any one of the following. Once you and your partner have completed, exchange the work with each other. Read each other’s work and provide critical feedback. 1. School Life v/s College Life.
answer:
SCHOOL LIFE V/S COLLEGE LIFE

School and college are two successive stages of education, and a student who passes from one to the other feels that the world has been turned upside down. Both are places of learning, both are entered through an examination, and both shape a young person’s future; yet they differ in freedom, responsibility and the style of teaching.

The similarities are easy to see. In both, the day is arranged around a timetable, a teacher stands in front of a class, examinations decide promotion and friendships are formed for life. Both stages teach languages, mathematics, science and social studies, and both demand punctuality, discipline and regular work. In both, a student who misses lessons must catch up on his own, and in both the annual result carries the same mixture of hope and fear.

The differences, however, are more striking. In school, a student wears a uniform, follows a fixed timetable and is watched over from assembly to home time; attendance is marked twice a day and parents are informed of every absence. In college, there is no uniform, attendance is checked only in the lecture hall, and the student must decide how to use the free periods. School teachers dictate notes and remind the class of deadlines; college teachers lecture, recommend readings and expect independent work. The school syllabus is small and the whole class moves together, while the college syllabus is wide, the pace is fast and the student chooses a specialisation. Finally, school friendships are made within one class, whereas college brings together students from many cities and backgrounds.

In short, school life trains a child while college life tests a young adult. School gives security, discipline and a common foundation; college gives freedom, choice and responsibility. The wise student enjoys the freedom of college without forgetting the habits learnt at school.
explanation: Model compare-contrast essay (about 300 words) following the structure taught in Exercise 1: introduction that develops a ground, body of similarities, body of differences, and a conclusion that restates the comparison. Connectors used: both, yet, however, whereas, while, in short.

question: Work with a partner and write compare-contrast essay on any one of the following. Once you and your partner have completed, exchange the work with each other. Read each other’s work and provide critical feedback. 2. Physical Games v/s Online Games.
answer:
PHYSICAL GAMES V/S ONLINE GAMES

Not long ago a game meant a ball, a field and a crowd of shouting friends. Today it often means a screen, a headset and a room with one person in it. Physical games and online games both entertain, both sharpen the mind and both build friendships, but in almost everything else they are opposites.

The similarities are real. Both have rules, strategy and a score; a cricketer and a gamer alike learn to read an opponent’s next move. Both offer competition and the pleasure of winning, and both can be played in teams. In both, a player improves only by playing regularly, and both can teach patience and concentration. Both, too, are ways of escaping boredom, and both give young people something to talk about with their friends.

The differences begin with the body. A physical game exercises the whole body — running, jumping, sweating and building stamina — while an online game exercises mainly the thumbs and the eyes. A physical game is played outdoors in fresh air and sunlight; an online game is played indoors, often late at night, in a fixed posture that strains the back and the eyes. Physical games teach a child to lose in front of others, to shake hands and to control anger; online games let a player hide behind an avatar and quit when losing. A physical game costs little beyond a ball and needs open ground; an online game needs electricity, a device and a connection, and can become expensive. Most important, a physical game ends when the players go home, whereas an online game has no natural ending and can swallow whole nights.

To sum up, both kinds of games have a place, but they are not interchangeable. Online games are convenient and often clever, yet nothing can replace the sun, the ground and the healthy tiredness of a physical game. A balanced life keeps the screen for an hour and the field for the evening.
explanation: Model compare-contrast essay (about 300 words) in the pattern of the sample: common ground in the introduction, one paragraph of similarities, one of differences, and a conclusion with a recommendation. Contrast is carried by while, whereas, yet and but.

question: Work with a partner and write compare-contrast essay on any one of the following. Once you and your partner have completed, exchange the work with each other. Read each other’s work and provide critical feedback. 3. Books v/s Mobile Phones
answer:
BOOKS V/S MOBILE PHONES

Two objects lie on the same table in a modern home: a printed book and a mobile phone. One is made of paper and glue, the other of glass and metal; one has been with us for five centuries, the other for barely two decades. Both carry words, both can teach and entertain, and yet they serve reading in very different ways.

The similarities are obvious. Both can hold a novel, a newspaper, a dictionary or a textbook; both let a reader mark a page, look up a word and return to a favourite passage. Both can be carried in a bag and read in a bus, and both give access to the world’s knowledge. For a student, a phone can even hold hundreds of books, which no school bag can.

The differences matter more. A book needs no battery, no signal and no password, so it never dies in the middle of a paragraph; a phone must be charged and can lose its network. A printed page is quiet and fixed, and nothing on it competes for attention, whereas a phone vibrates with notifications and draws the eye to messages, videos and games. Reading on paper is slower and deeper, and we tend to remember printed pages better; reading on a screen is faster and more scattered. A book can be lent, gifted and inherited, while a phone’s library disappears with the device or the account. Finally, a printed book costs money once, whereas a phone invites continuous spending on data, apps and subscriptions.

In conclusion, the phone is a wonderful library and a dangerous rival to reading. It can carry a thousand books, but it can also stop us from finishing one. The sensible reader uses the screen for what only a screen can do, and keeps a printed book for the pleasure that no notification can interrupt.
explanation: Model compare-contrast essay (about 300 words). It uses the point-by-point pattern, develops a ground in the introduction (both carry words and knowledge), treats similarities before differences, and closes with a balanced judgement rather than a one-sided verdict.

question: Now, work in pairs and discuss orally the following conversation of Aakash and Dharti on Nature. Identify how the phrases of sharing information and ideas are used.
answer:
PHRASES OF SHARING INFORMATION AND IDEAS IN THE DIALOGUE

No. | Phrase in the dialogue | Speaker | Category in the table | Function in the conversation
1 | “I’m afraid I’ve got some bad news that air pollution could ruin our nature completely.” | Aakash | Phrase to share bad news (“I’m afraid I’ve got some bad news…”) | opens the topic and warns Dharti that what follows is unpleasant, so the listener is prepared
2 | “My goodness! Can you tell me in detail?” | Dharti | Responding to disturbing information | expresses shock and asks for more, which keeps the sharing going
3 | “That’s awful! How is the air getting polluted?” | Dharti | Responding to disturbing information (“That’s awful / a pity / unfortunate”) | shows sympathy with the news and invites explanation
4 | “Yeah, I know that.” / “Yeah, deforestation has been a huge problem nowadays.” | Dharti | Active listening (a supporting move, not a phrase from the table) | proves she is following the news and adds her own point to Aakash’s
5 | “Sounds great! That could be a good effort to save our nature and keep the planet clean.” | Dharti | Responding to exciting information or idea (“Sounds great!”) | approves Aakash’s suggestion of using paper bags and states why it is good
6 | “So, let’s do it from today.” | Aakash | Making a suggestion / closing the sharing | turns information into an agreed action
7 | “Of course. Thank you for sharing a valuable information.” | Dharti | Thanking and closing | acknowledges the information politely and ends the exchange
8 | “You are welcome. See you again.” / “Bye.” | Aakash / Dharti | Leave-taking | closes the conversation courteously

The dialogue therefore follows a clear pattern: share the news (bad or good), respond with feeling, ask for details, add information, suggest an action, agree, thank and close. The phrases from the table do the work of each step: “I’m afraid I’ve got some bad news…” opens, “My goodness!” and “That’s awful!” respond, and “Sounds great!” approves the idea.
explanation: The task asks students to identify, not to invent, the phrases. Each item is matched to one of the four rows of the table on book page 27 (sharing exciting news, responding to exciting news, sharing bad news, responding to disturbing news), and its function in the exchange is explained.

question: Work in groups of 2-3. Discuss one of the topics given below as assigned by the teacher. One of you should note all the discussed points. Make sure that every group member is participating in the discussion. 1. Examination Results
answer:
GROUP DISCUSSION NOTES — Topic 1: Examination Results

Group of three: Ayesha (chair), Bilal, Hina (note-taker).

1. Sharing the news. Ayesha: “I have got a bit of news to tell you. Our annual result is expected on the 15th, three days earlier than the date announced.” Bilal: “That sounds like great news, but I am a little nervous about the mathematics paper.” Hina: “Lucky you! I have to reappear in two subjects.”

2. How results are received. Ayesha: a result is a milestone, not a verdict on a student’s ability. Bilal: comparison with cousins and neighbours creates more pressure than the paper itself. Hina: a single bad paper can destroy a student’s confidence for years.

3. Problems noted. (a) Parents compare marks instead of effort; (b) students hide results or alter marksheets out of fear; (c) tuition centres promise grades rather than understanding; (d) failures are mocked on social media; (e) re-checking and re-totalling facilities are not understood by many families.

4. Suggestions. (a) Discuss the result calmly at home and praise effort; (b) use the re-checking window if marks are unexpectedly low; (c) plan the next year’s study from the mistakes in the answer script; (d) celebrate a friend’s success without boasting about one’s own; (e) support a classmate who has failed instead of avoiding him.

5. Conclusion. All three agreed that a result is one photograph of one day, not the whole story of a student. Hard work, honesty and the willingness to learn from mistakes matter more than a single percentage.
explanation: Open-ended group-discussion task; the notes are a model of what the note-taker should record: speakers, points raised under headings, and the group’s agreed conclusion. The phrases of sharing news and responding to it (“I have got a bit of news…”, “That sounds like great news”, “Lucky you!”, “I’m sorry to hear that”) are used naturally.

question: Work in groups of 2-3. Discuss one of the topics given below as assigned by the teacher. One of you should note all the discussed points. Make sure that every group member is participating in the discussion. 2. A Sensational Cricket Match
answer:
GROUP DISCUSSION NOTES — Topic 2: A Sensational Cricket Match

Group of three: Bilal (chair), Hina, Ayesha (note-taker).

1. Sharing the news. Bilal: “I have got some great news for you. Pakistan won the final by one wicket off the last ball.” Hina: “Oh, how wonderful! I could not watch the last over.” Ayesha: “Incredible! Tell us everything.”

2. The match in brief. Pakistan needed six runs from the last two balls; the number eight batsman hit a six over long-on; the bowler had taken four wickets earlier; the fielding side dropped two catches in the final over.

3. Why it was sensational. (a) The result was decided on the last ball; (b) an unlikely batsman became the hero; (c) the crowd’s noise could be heard outside the stadium; (d) the match swung three times in the last five overs; (e) the winning six was replayed on every screen in the bazaar.

4. Lessons drawn. (a) A game is never over until the last ball; (b) a team wins because the lower order contributes, not only the stars; (c) dropped catches cost matches; (d) the losing captain’s grace in defeat was as impressive as the win.

5. Conclusion. The group agreed that the match was memorable not only for the six but for the nerve shown under pressure, and that such matches are why cricket is followed so passionately in Pakistan.
explanation: Open-ended discussion task. The model notes show the note-taker’s job — recording each speaker’s contribution and the group’s agreed points — and use the “exciting news” phrases from the table (“I have got some great news for you”, “Oh, how wonderful!”, “Incredible!”).

question: Work in groups of 2-3. Discuss one of the topics given below as assigned by the teacher. One of you should note all the discussed points. Make sure that every group member is participating in the discussion. 3. Loss of Job During Pandemic
answer:
GROUP DISCUSSION NOTES — Topic 3: Loss of Job During Pandemic

Group of three: Hina (chair), Ayesha, Bilal (note-taker).

1. Sharing the news. Hina: “I’m afraid I’ve got some bad news. My uncle, who worked in a textile mill in Karachi, lost his job last month when the factory reduced its staff.” Ayesha: “I’m awfully sorry to hear that. That must be awful for his family.” Bilal: “I know how you must be feeling. My neighbour is in the same position.”

2. Causes noted. (a) Lockdowns closed markets and factories; (b) export orders were cancelled; (c) mills ran short time and then retrenched workers; (d) daily-wage earners were the first to be sent home; (e) most families had no savings.

3. Effects noted. (a) School fees unpaid and children at risk of leaving school; (b) borrowing from relatives and shopkeepers; (c) stress and quarrels at home; (d) some families migrated back to their villages; (e) skilled workers took up low-paid work.

4. What helped. (a) The government’s cash-relief programme; (b) ration from the mosque and the community; (c) a small tailoring business run from home by the women of the family; (d) a neighbour who recommended the uncle for a job in a smaller mill.

5. Suggestions. (a) Keep an emergency fund equal to three months’ income; (b) learn a skill that can earn from home; (c) register with the labour department and keep identity and service documents safe; (d) form a workers’ committee to deal with the employer collectively; (e) treat the unemployed with respect, not pity.

6. Conclusion. The group agreed that job loss in a pandemic is a social problem as much as an economic one, and that family, community and government support must work together.
explanation: Open-ended discussion task. The notes are a model record of the discussion and deliberately use the “bad news” phrases of the table (“I’m afraid I’ve got some bad news…”, “I’m awfully sorry to hear that”, “That must be awful”, “I know how you must be feeling”), which is the language the unit is teaching.

question: Work in groups of 2-3. Discuss one of the topics given below as assigned by the teacher. One of you should note all the discussed points. Make sure that every group member is participating in the discussion. 4. Electricity shortage
answer:
GROUP DISCUSSION NOTES — Topic 4: Electricity Shortage

Group of three: Ayesha (chair), Bilal, Hina (note-taker).

1. Opening the topic. Ayesha: “I regret to inform you that our area faced eight hours of load-shedding yesterday, and the exams are next week.” Bilal: “That’s terrible. My younger brother studied by candlelight.” Hina: “Too bad! We lost a whole evening of preparation.”

2. Causes noted. (a) Demand rises in summer because of air-conditioners; (b) old transmission lines lose power; (c) circular debt prevents fuel purchase; (d) theft and illegal connections; (e) limited hydropower in winter and costly imported fuel.

3. Effects noted. (a) Students cannot study or attend online classes; (b) small shops and tailoring units lose working hours; (c) hospitals and vaccination fridges are at risk; (d) water pumps stop, so drinking water becomes scarce; (e) generators and inverters add to air and noise pollution.

4. Suggestions. (a) Repair and upgrade transmission lines; (b) shift to solar panels, especially for schools and clinics; (c) publish a load-management schedule and follow it honestly; (d) punish power theft and recover dues from defaulters; (e) use LED bulbs and switch off unnecessary appliances; (f) build the Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand dams for cheap hydropower.

5. Conclusion. The group agreed that the shortage is partly a supply problem and partly a habit problem: the country must produce more electricity and must also stop wasting what it produces.
explanation: Open-ended discussion task. The model notes give points under cause, effect and solution headings, as a note-taker would, and use the phrases for sharing and responding to disturbing information (“I regret to inform you that…”, “That’s terrible”, “Too bad!”).

question: Exercise 3 — [first line missing in the printed book] about topic in the class. Kemenber to use phrases given above.
answer:
MODEL ORAL TALK ON THE UNIT TOPIC “PRESERVATION OF NATURE”

Good morning, everyone. I have got a bit of news to tell you, and I am afraid it is not all good news. Our city’s only lake has lost half of its fish this year, and the reason is the waste we throw into it.

I regret to inform you that the tests found plastic, detergent and factory oil in the water. That is awful, but it is not the end of the story, and that is the good news I want to share. Last month a group of students of our school cleaned one kilometre of the bank. I have got some great news for you: in six weeks the birds have come back, and the water at that end is clear again.

Our plan is simple. First, each class will adopt one stretch of the bank and clean it every Friday. Second, we will ask the shopkeepers near the lake to sell paper bags instead of plastic ones. Third, we will plant fifty saplings along the path before the rains. When our teacher heard the plan, she said, “What a fantastic idea!”

So, let us begin this Friday at eight o’clock. Thank you for listening, and I hope you will all join us.
explanation: The printed Exercise 3 is defective: only one line survives (“about topic in the class. Kemenber to use phrases given above.”) — the opening line and the topic list are missing, and “Kemenber” is a misprint of “Remember”. The stem is kept as printed. The model answer therefore supplies what the surviving instruction asks for: a short oral talk delivered in class on the unit topic, using the phrases of sharing information and ideas (“I have got a bit of news to tell you”, “I’m afraid it is not all good news”, “I regret to inform you that”, “That is awful”, “I have got some great news for you”, “What a fantastic idea!”).

question: (i) All the shops in our area used to be closed during the lockdown now they’re open all day.
answer: All the shops in our area used to be closed during the lockdown; now they’re open all day.
explanation: The sentence contains two independent clauses — “All the shops … lockdown” and “now they’re open all day” — with no conjunction between them. Rule 1 allows a semicolon to join two related complete thoughts, so it replaces the missing full stop: “… lockdown; now they’re open all day.”

question: (ii) The government has wiped out all encroachments consequently the roads outside the shopping malls have become wider.
answer: The government has wiped out all encroachments; consequently, the roads outside the shopping malls have become wider.
explanation: “Consequently” is a conjunctive adverb, so Rule 2 applies: a semicolon is placed before it and a comma after it, joining the two independent clauses. A comma alone before “consequently” would be a comma splice.

question: (iii) Because there was heavy fog in the morning the services at the airport were closed.
answer: Because there was heavy fog in the morning, the services at the airport were closed. (No semicolon is needed in this sentence.)
explanation: A semicolon may join only two independent clauses. Here the first part, “Because there was heavy fog in the morning”, is a dependent (subordinate) clause, so it cannot be separated from its main clause by a semicolon; it is closed with a comma instead. If the writer wished to use a semicolon, the “Because” would have to go: “There was heavy fog in the morning; the services at the airport were closed.”

question: (iv) Babar was not excited about his seventeenth birthday however his spirits improved when he opened his presents.
answer: Babar was not excited about his seventeenth birthday; however, his spirits improved when he opened his presents.
explanation: “However” is a conjunctive adverb linking two independent clauses, so Rule 2 applies: semicolon before “however”, comma after it. Without the semicolon the sentence would be a comma splice or a run-on.

question: Work in pairs and fix the errors in the use of semicolon in the following paragraph. After completing, share your work with your partner.
answer:
CORRECTED PARAGRAPH

A good student is the one who is punctual, regular, and hard working; moreover, he has to be obedient to the teachers and respectful to class fellows. Teachers have to play a large part; the parents are equally responsible for developing such qualities. It goes beyond doubt that a nation’s destiny is made in class rooms; therefore, the co-ordination between the teachers and the parents is a must so that the destiny makers should be led in the right direction. The world is growing more competitive with the passage of time, and in this context, our present generation and the coming generations have to be jointly prepared by us.

CORRECTIONS MADE

No. | Printed | Corrected | Reason
1 | “… hard working, moreover, he has to be obedient …” | “… hard working; moreover, he has to be obedient …” | “Moreover” is a conjunctive adverb joining two independent clauses: semicolon before it, comma after it (Rule 2).
2 | “Teachers have to play a large part, the parents are equally responsible …” | “Teachers have to play a large part; the parents are equally responsible …” | Two independent clauses with no conjunction: a semicolon is required (Rule 1).
3 | “… makes in class rooms, therefore, the co-ordination …” | “… is made in class rooms; therefore, the co-ordination …” | “Therefore” is a conjunctive adverb, so it takes a semicolon before and a comma after (Rule 2). The verb “makes” is also repaired to the passive “is made”, because a destiny is made, not makes.
4 | “… the co-ordination … is must …” | “… the co-ordination … is a must …” | A separate slip of grammar, not of punctuation: “must” is used here as a noun and needs the article.

Points 1-3 are the punctuation errors the exercise asks for. The paragraph as printed contains no semicolon at all; commas are doing the work that semicolons should do, which is why it reads as a series of run-on sentences.
explanation: The exercise is about the semicolon only. Each place where two independent clauses meet either without a conjunction (Rule 1) or with a conjunctive adverb (Rule 2) must take a semicolon; the adverb is then followed by a comma. The other small slip (“is must” → “is a must”) is corrected and flagged separately so that the student can see which change belongs to the punctuation exercise.

question: Work in pairs and read the following text. Spot errors of regular and irregular verbs where necessary in the article given below.
answer:
VERB ERRORS IN THE ARTICLE ON ROBERT GODDARD

No. | Printed form | Correction | Reason
1 | “he become interested in firecrackers” | “he became interested in firecrackers” | The past tense of “become” is “became” (become — became — become); the paragraph is in the past tense.
2 | “the other professors laugh at him” | “the other professors laughed at him” | Past tense needed to match “went back”, “failed attempts”; “laugh” is the present form.
3 | “When the New York Times sawed his article” | “When the New York Times saw his article” | The past of “see” is “saw” (see — saw — seen). “Sawed” is the past of the different verb “saw”, to cut with a saw.
4 | “Goddard want to prove” | “Goddard wanted to prove” | Past tense of “want” is “wanted”; the surrounding narrative is in the past.
5 | “putted it into an open car” | “put it into an open car” | “Put” is irregular and does not change: put — put — put. “Putt” with “putted” belongs to golf.
6 | “and drived to his aunt’s nearby farm” | “and drove to his aunt’s nearby farm” | “Drive” is irregular: drive — drove — driven; “drived” does not exist.
7 | “and light the fuse” | “and lit the fuse” | Past of “light” is “lit” (light — lit — lit); “light” is the present form.
8 | “Then it felled into the field” | “Then it fell into the field” | “Fall” is irregular: fall — fell — fallen. “Felled” is the past of “fell”, to cut down a tree, and is wrong here.
9 | “after he become successful” | “after he became successful” | Same error as No. 1: the past “became” is required.

Corrected sentences, in order: “When he was a child, he became interested in firecrackers …”; “the other professors laughed at him”; “When the New York Times saw his article …”; “Goddard wanted to prove that the New York Times was wrong”; “he built a ten-foot rocket, put it into an open car, and drove to his aunt’s nearby farm”; “He put the rocket in a field and lit the fuse”; “Then it fell into the field”; “No one made fun of him after he became successful.”

Forms that are already correct and should not be changed: was born, thought, later became, built, took, went, failed, wrote, believed, would be, had, reported, was, made (fun).
explanation: Nine verb forms are wrong, and all of them are either an irregular verb given its regular “-ed” form (sawed, putted, drived, felled) or a present form left in a past-tense narrative (become x2, laugh, want, light). “His work did not stop” and “didn’t fly” are acceptable and are not counted as errors.

question: Work individually, and fill in the blanks with an appropriate verb form of the verbs given in brackets.
answer:
VERB FORMS FOR THE PASSAGE ON AJRAK

No. | Verb in brackets | Answer | Form and reason
1 | appreciate | is appreciated | Present simple passive: “It is appreciated … throughout Pakistan” (the subject “It” receives the action).
2 | be | are | Present simple, plural subject “The motif and patterns”; the passive that follows needs “are”.
3 | produce | produced | Past participle in the passive “are traditionally produced by resist block printing”.
4 | manufacture | manufactured | Past participle in the passive “Ajrak is manufactured in various blends of deep crimson …”.
5 | complete | completed | Past participle in the passive “the process … is completed almost in thirty days”.
6 | coil | coiled | Past participle in the passive “cloth is coiled … on a copper vat”.
7 | wrap | wrapped | Past participle in the passive, parallel to “coiled”: “is coiled and wrapped”.
8 | soak | soaked | Past participle in the passive, parallel to “coiled” and “wrapped”: “and then soaked in Eruca Sativa seed oil”.
9 | do | done | Past participle in the passive “is done” (do — did — done).
10 | protect | protects | Present simple active, third person singular, subject “This process”.
11 | dip | dipped | Past participle in the passive ellipsis “when dipped in the alizarin dye” (= when it is dipped).
12 | be | is | Present simple passive “fabric is dipped in alizarin in a copper vat”.
13 | use | used | Past participle in the passive “Camel dung is used to remove excess tanning”.
14 | facilitate | facilitate | Base form after “help to bleach … and also facilitate …”; the second verb is a bare infinitive coordinated with “bleach” after “help to”.

Completed passage: “Ajrak is a symbol of rich Sindhi culture and icon of love. It is appreciated as such throughout Pakistan. … The motif and patterns on Ajrak are traditionally produced by resist block printing … Ajrak is manufactured in various blends of deep crimson and other defused blue colours. The production of traditional Ajrak is a complex process comprising twenty one stages and completed almost in thirty days, by using only indigenous materials. Cut to size cloth is coiled and wrapped on a copper vat and then soaked in Eruca Sativa seed oil for fifteen days. First printing of the white outline of the pattern by paste of lime and Acacia gum is done … This process protects the part of cloth to get imprinted and rest of areas turn crimson when dipped in the alizarin dye. … water soaked fabric is dipped in alizarin in a copper vat … Camel dung is used to remove excess tanning … Alternate drenching and drying help to bleach the fabric and also facilitate the maturing of the colours.”
explanation: Almost the whole passage describes a process, so the passive voice dominates: “is/are + past participle” (appreciated, produced, manufactured, completed, coiled, wrapped, soaked, done, dipped, used). Only two blanks are active — “This process protects …” and “help to bleach … and also facilitate …” — because the process itself is the doer. The printed passage also contains the unrelated slips “to becomes deep in tone” and “defused blue colours” (for “diffused”), which lie outside the blanks; they belong to the proof-reading of the text, not to this exercise.
